options.label: ■ square
options.feedback: Yes! The unit is circle, square — and after a circle comes a square.

options.label: ● circle
options.feedback: Look at what comes after each circle in the pattern. Is it another circle?

options.label: ▲ triangle
options.feedback: There are no triangles in this pattern. Which shapes repeat?

hints: Say the pattern out loud: circle, square, circle, square, …
What always comes after a circle?
exercises.solution: The unit is ● ■ (circle, square), repeating. The last item shown is a circle, so the next item is a **square** ■.

exercises.prompt: Here is a repeating pattern: 🍎 🍌 🍌 🍎 🍌 🍌 🍎 🍌 🍌 … What is its **unit** — the part that repeats?

options.feedback: If the unit were just 🍎, the pattern would be 🍎 🍎 🍎 … Look at what comes after each apple.
If the unit were 🍎 🍌, the third item would be 🍎. But the third item is 🍌.
Yes! Apple, banana, banana — three items that repeat again and again.
The bananas are part of the unit, but the apple repeats too. What is the whole part that repeats?

hints: Find where the pattern starts again: where does the second 🍎 appear?
Everything from the first 🍎 up to just before the second 🍎 is the unit.
exercises.solution: The pattern starts again at the fourth item, the second 🍎. So the unit is everything before it: **🍎 🍌 🍌**, three items. A unit is the whole part that repeats, not a single item.

feedback.message: The pattern does not add 1. How much bigger is each number than the one before?
Doubling 8 gives 16, but look again: 2 to 4 to 6 — is that doubling, or adding the same number each time?

hints: How do you get from 2 to 4? From 4 to 6?
The rule is "add 2". What is 8 + 2?
exercises.solution: Each number is 2 more than the one before: the rule is **add 2**. So after 8 comes $8 + 2 = $ **10**.

exercises.prompt: The pattern 5, 10, 15, 20, … adds 5 each time. What is the **6th** number in the pattern?

feedback.message: 25 is the 5th number. Count the numbers carefully: 5 is the 1st, 10 is the 2nd, … Which is the 6th?
We want the 6th *number in the pattern*, not the number 6. Keep adding 5.

hints: Point to each number and say its place: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, …
exercises.solution: Keep adding 5: 5 (1st), 10 (2nd), 15 (3rd), 20 (4th), 25 (5th), **30** (6th). You can also see that the $n$-th number is $5 \times n$, so the 6th is $5 \times 6 = 30$.

exercises.prompt: Thandi's necklace goes red, blue, green, red, blue, green, … What colour is **bead 20**?

options.label: Red
options.feedback: Every third bead is green: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18. Bead 19 starts a new unit. What comes after that?

options.label: Blue
options.feedback: Yes! Bead 18 is green, bead 19 starts a new unit with red, and bead 20 is blue.

options.label: Green
options.feedback: Green beads are at 3, 6, 9, … Is 20 in the count by threes?

hints: Every third bead is green. Count in threes: 3, 6, 9, …
Which is the last green bead before 20? Then count on.
exercises.solution: The unit has 3 beads, so the green beads are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, … Bead 18 is green, bead 19 is red and bead 20 is **blue**. (For grown-ups: $20 = 3 \times 6 + 2$, so bead 20 matches bead 2.)

exercises.prompt: Today is **Wednesday**. What day of the week will it be in **14 days**?

options.label: Wednesday
options.feedback: Yes! 14 days is exactly two weeks, and after every 7 days the week starts again.

options.label: Thursday
options.feedback: That would be 1 day later (or 8, or 15). How many whole weeks are 14 days?

options.label: Tuesday
options.feedback: Think of the week as a pattern with a unit of 7 days. How many units are 14 days?

hints: The days of the week repeat with a unit of 7 days.
14 days is how many whole weeks?
exercises.solution: The week repeats every 7 days. 14 days is exactly 2 weeks, so we land on the same day: **Wednesday**.

exercises.prompt: A clapping game goes: *clap, clap, stamp, clap, clap, stamp, …* In the first **12** moves, how many **claps** are there?

feedback.message: 4 is the number of *stamps*. The question asks about claps.
Each unit has 2 claps and 1 stamp. How many units fit in 12 moves?
Not every move is a clap — every third move is a stamp.

hints: The unit is clap, clap, stamp: 3 moves with 2 claps.
12 moves make 4 units. How many claps is that?
exercises.solution: The unit *clap, clap, stamp* has 3 moves. 12 moves make 4 units (3, 6, 9, 12), and each unit has 2 claps. So there are $2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = $ **8** claps (and 4 stamps).

exercises.prompt: A pattern starts **1, 2, 4, …** Nia says the next number is **8**. Diego says it is **7**. Who could be right?

options.label: Only Nia — the numbers are doubling
options.feedback: Doubling fits 1, 2, 4. But Diego's rule, add 1, then 2, then 3, fits too!

options.label: Only Diego
options.feedback: Diego's rule fits, but so does Nia's doubling rule.

options.label: Both, as long as each says their rule
options.feedback: Yes! Doubling gives 8 and "add one more each time" gives 7. The first few items do not decide the pattern.

options.label: Neither
options.feedback: Check Nia's rule: 1 doubled is 2, 2 doubled is 4, 4 doubled is 8. It fits!

hints: Does doubling fit 1, 2, 4? Does adding 1, then 2, then 3 fit?
Can two different rules start the same way?
exercises.solution: **Both** could be right. Doubling: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … Adding one more each time: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, … Both rules fit the first three numbers. That is why a pattern needs its rule to be stated.

exercises.prompt: Gideon's game: true or false? *"In any repeating pattern whose unit has 4 items, item 5 and item 9 are the same."*

options.label: True
options.feedback: Yes! Item 9 is 4 places after item 5, and 4 places on, the pattern is always back to the same item.

options.label: False
options.feedback: How far apart are items 5 and 9? Compare that with the size of the unit.

hints: How many places apart are item 5 and item 9?
In a pattern whose unit has 4 items, what is true about the item 4 places further on?
exercises.solution: **True.** Item 9 is exactly 4 places after item 5, and the unit has 4 items, so item 9 is the same as item 5. (Both are also the same as item 1.) This works for *every* pattern with a 4-item unit — Lean proves the general fact in the lesson.

exercises.prompt: Margaret's computer checked the remainder shortcut for beads 1 to 1,000 and found no mistakes. Can we be sure the shortcut works for bead 5,000 too?

options.label: Only if the computer checks bead 5,000 as well
options.feedback: Checking more beads gives more evidence, but there would always be another bead. Is there a reason that covers them all?

options.label: Yes — the reason (jumps of one whole unit never change the colour) works for every bead
options.feedback: Exactly! The computer's check is good evidence for 1,000 beads; the reason is a proof for every bead, including bead 5,000.

options.label: No — we can never know anything about bead 5,000
options.feedback: We can! The lesson explains *why* the shortcut works, and that reason does not depend on which bead we pick.

hints: Does the reason in "Why predicting works" depend on which bead we look at?
What is the difference between checking examples and having a reason?
exercises.solution: **Yes.** The computer checked 1,000 beads — evidence for those beads. But the reason in the lesson works for any bead: jumping by a whole unit of 3 beads never changes the colour, so only the leftover steps matter. That reason (proved in Lean) covers bead 5,000 and every other bead.
